I picked up Layers of Fear after I noticed it had come out of early access. I refuse to buy games in early access anymore, so I just add them to my wish lish and wait for them to be "finished".

I am posting this review after I played and beat the game.

Layers of fear is kind of an interactive story, puzzle, survival horror kind of game. You play as an artist returning home to work on his opus magnum.

At what first appears to be a basic jaunt around his home, quickly turns into a psychological horror, the house appears to be (possibly) haunted as the layouts change, you are confronted by visions of your dead wife and other various paranormal-esc situations.

Along the way, you'll collect notes and other memorabilia within the house that offers quick glimpses into the painter's past life, his family and even the state of his mental health. 

The game isn't as "scary" as other games of this nature may be and in fact, you are put in several situations in which you can avoid confrontation entirely if so desired. As far as I am aware, there isn't really a way to die in the traditional sense, which is nice, because the game is set up in a way that you won't have to restart entire chapters of a mistake you may have made. 

The writing for the story is farily good, I'd say much better then games such as Penumbra. It's a fairly unqiue and engaging story that made me want to continue playing just to find out a little bit more. 

The puzzles are (generally) not too hard and there was very few moments I was actually stuck. Unfortunately the game doesn't help you in any real sense, besides some hints scattered about the game and as a result some of the more obscure puzzles can leave players scratching their head.

While I did enjoy the time I spent with the game, there are issues with it that I feel inclined to inform people of. 

For starters, when you first start playing the game, it's fun and fascinating to explore the artist's big, beautiful house. The problem is that very early in the game, the exploration aspect of the game is all but removed, Instead the game becomes somewhat of an "on-rails" adventure game, instead of walking freely through the house, instead you'll be traversing hallways and single rooms. 9 out of 10 times, as you enter one room, the door will close and lock behind you, denying any sort of back tracking in the game. 

This can become an issue, because the game feels as if it were meant to be explored and it was just a concept that was throw to the side. On occasion you may be given the opportunity to travel off the beaten path, but it is almost always just for a moment and it usually results in a dead end or locked door. The missing exploration concept bothers me, because I have always loved horror books, games and movies that involved big, old, beautiful mansions.

Another problem that I had with the game is it never really changes scenery too much. A large majority of the game just looks the same. Expect to see a lot of dark, dingy rooms, broken walls and floors and broken furniture. Also expect to see the same art, furniture and random junk over and over and over again. This becomes an even bigger issue when the game starts to begin recycling rooms. 

Finally, the last problem I had with the game was the story. Remember earlier when I said they had a good story? They do, the problem stems from the fact that there's a lot of information presented for players to process and it's never really tied together or explained in any real sort of meaningful way. While I enjoyed the game while I played it, after I beat it, I felt very dissatisfied because I really didn't learn all that much and the game doesn't really make a good attempt at helping you understand. 

I have questions, no one appears to have answers and frankly, I am no really into the entire "fan theory community" in which the developers of a game simply don't inform or release information to players, instead they just wait to see if someone gets it "right". For me, it just seems like a really lazy form of writing and I tend to get high aggravated with it.

Don't get me wrong, I love reading long books, I like guessing at the story, or the plots or even coming up with theories as I enjoy whatever book/movie/game I am playing. But I expect the writers to eventually tie down and explain what is going on in a clear, concise and satisfying way.

If you like games of this nature, if you have enjoyed games like 'A Machine for Pigs' and 'Penumbra', you'll enjoy this game a lot. If you like psychological horror, you'll appreciate this game. I can without hesitation recommend this game to horror fans, even given the rough spots of the game.

[h1] The Story: [/h1]
It's the early 1900s, and "the Master Painter" has returned to his seemingly abandoned home to finish painting his magnum opus. Take control of the masterpainter, and follow him on his journey as he furiously masterpaints all over his house. Watch as he masterpaints and coats the walls in his creative juices. Assemble sentimental objects to help aid in the masterpainter's masterpainting. Collect old notes from his wife about how his chronic masterpainting has ruined their marriage. Bear witness to the adverse effects that a masterpainting addiction has on your mental health. Can you help cure the masterpainter of his masterpainting addiction, or will he shoot his biggest, most creative load of all time?

[h1] What I Thought: [/h1]
Layers of Fear tells a cliche story, but it tells it very well. To its credit, it doesn't seem to be trying to reinvent the wheel when it comes to story telling. What it does do, and it does this very well, is create an amazingly terrifying atmosphere that is guaranteed to unnerve even the most seasoned horror game fans.

The setting is nothing new, but the concept is: It's your stereotypical haunted house simulator with a literally artistic twist. The rooms you progress through are randomly generated. This helps keep the game fresh if you're one of those completionist types who needs to replay games to find all the collectibles. Beyond that it's mostly just a gimmick, but a welcome one at that. The house is beautifully crafted and the atmosphere is very thick. The sound design is extremely well done, and It's easy to get lost (figuratively and literally) in the world of the Master Painter.

Speaking of the Master Painter, the guy is a total scumbag. What we learn of him doesn't [i] paint [/i] a pretty picture. He's an abusive, neglectful alcoholic who, as metioned earlier, does nothing but masterpaint all day. It's impossible to identify with him in any way, unless the player has an affinity for art. The voice acting feels off... that's not to say it's bad, it's just that it doesn't seem to fit the character that the developers are presenting to us. All in all, the protagonist is interesting, but he's mostly just a flanderized "tortured artist" type of guy.

I would definitely recommend this game to horror fans. It's a must play. I'm hesitant to recommend it to adventure enthusiasts, as the story is shaping up to be very cliche and predictable, but you should give it a try if you're at all interested. It's definitely something people should experience.

Now if you'll all excuse me, I'm going to go browse ArtHub and masterpaint.

If you require a great example of what the Unity engine can do [i]Layers of Fear[/i] is an excellent one. What with all the asset flipping done in the industry lately this game is a refreshing experience.

[b]Victorian-era madness[/b]

Our protagonist is a painter who has seen better days. We return to his mansion and start exploring it only to, eventually, find a canvas hiding his [i]Magnum Opus[/i]. This masterpiece, however, is incomplete, so our job will be to recover the items needed to finally realise his greatest work.

Throughout the 6 chapters of the game we are plunged into a nightmarish version of our home. We look for mementos of our family, remember key moments by picking us personal effects of ours or those of our wife and, well, we try to survive. Since this is mainly a walking simulator dying is next to impossible, however, the encounters we experience (and the doors we enter) determine the outcome. The game offers 3 different (and very exciting) endings.

[b]Psychological horror at its best[/b]

As we venture through the house we see it constantly changing. Paintings (and often other objects) keep melting, a ghost frequently appears and tries to grab us, corridors become longer and darker, objects float and fly through the rooms and there's many more! Our best bet is to try to interact with everything possible (opening, for instance, every single drawer to find a new note) so that we can get to know more of the background story.

[b]In Unity We Trust[/b]

The game utilises the Unity engine very well and showcases it as much as it can. The melting paintings look great (they often reveal another painting underneath), and pretty much the entire game is done right and we truly believe we are in a house built in the Victorian era. Attention to detail is excellent and I would like to note that finally this is another of those first person games where we do have a reflection in the mirror. Performance-wise I was at a solid 60 FPS at all times, however, sometimes I experienced regular stuttering (at one point I needed to quit and re-launch the game for it to stop).

[b]Indie game done right[/b]

Depending on the mementos and objects we find and based on how we react when faced with encounters the game offers 3 different endings. That's 3 playthroughs for you at least and you may want to do some more if you missed picking up just one of the many collectibles. The voice acting is acceptable during the narrative sequences and the game's soundtrack and overall atmosphere is so good that using a headset is a must.

Layers of Fear falls squarely in the psychological (some my say psychedelic) horror genre, from Polish indie developers Bloober. The game features a dark – sometimes too dark – environment, truly twisted visuals, some fantastically hair-raising moments, and a unique take on field of view that masterfully turns the haunted house into a claustrophobic Winchester house of terror. For a short jaunt into madness at about $4, it’s highly recommendable and entertaining.

Heavily inspired by The picture of Dorian Grey authored by Oscar Wilde.

As the description says, you take the role of an artist who is travelling through his house on a mission to finish his masterpiece, as you progress through the game, its begins to become darker & much more twisted, revealing bits and pieces of the storyline to you over time.

Pros

- Extremely immersive in terms of visual & audial prowess, the creators of this game dedicated alot of time towards ensuring it caem out looking & sounding gorgeous, not only that, but the amount of detail that has been put into the artwork and architecture really portrays some amazing talent within the fields.

- Immaculateley timed. The creators of this game have tried and tested every scare tactic. Theres is a perfect mix between jump scares & drawn out horror. Play this game at night alone and you will s**t yourself.

- Extremely well done storyline. The game offers you insights towards what has occured yet it manages to hold off the suspense by adding twists that you would never expect, ensuring that you will not be able to fully guess the plot until the very end of the game.

Cons

- There are a few graphical bugs, though not that many. Antialiasing is a problem at the moment as you will tend to notice most objects surrounding your character are jagged at the edges.

Altogether this game is a must have, the concept is fantastically original. It is definetley worth the 13 USD if you are a fan of survival horror, for it is a game that you shall never forget.

10/10

Layers of Fear is a horror adventure game that delves into the twisted mind of a troubled painter and his descent to madness. One thing I’ve notice the game does right is the pacing of the story. It starts of slow, depicting an earlier and happier life of the protagonist, introducing key objects and areas that will become central to the story later on. Gradually, the terror is introduced, first as harmless dissolving paintings, then to the ghastly apparition of his supposedly dearly departed wife. 

It’s great to see an early access horror game actually terrify me because I absolutely love the disturbing atmosphere and the tension I’ve felt traversing through the shifting and looping corridors of this mad painter’s house. The game is riddled with jumpscares, I’ll give you that one and I grew numb to them by the 3rd time but the game doesn’t solely rely on jumpscares to scare you. It incorporates sounds as a way to rattle you. Whether it is the haunting laughter of a distant woman or the mocking giggles of children, to the peaceful pieces of classical music, these sounds alerts the player and puts them on edge.  

There are barely any puzzles so this first person narrative is all you have but it isn’t exactly a walking simulator. There are notes to collect, objects to find that trigger memories and rooms that paint a story of the painter’s history.  I can’t say there’s much to explore since the game does lead you to where you need to go anyways so it is pretty much a linear game but it is enjoyable walking through the hallways of the painter’s home and see what has change since it does loop around (similar to PT, if you've played it).

Unfortunately, there are some optimization problems even though the graphics are pretty to look at (slows down in some parts i.e. the kitchen area) but nothing a few patches can’t solve. The early access only show about half of the game (from what I can tell) and I managed to complete it in an hour and half so I can’t imagine the full game will be too long. Then again, I can’t be certain since it’s not complete yet. I know some people aren’t keen on buying into an Early Access game but I bought it at a discount and I don’t regret my purchase. 

TL:DR

Pros: 
     -	Great, eerie atmosphere
     -	Excellent pacing of the story
     -	Good sounds and music
     -	Pretty graphics

Cons:
     -	Not complete yet since it is still in Early Access
     -	Optimization problems
     -	Jumpscares (I didn’t like them…)
     -	The slow pacing at the beginning might turn off some people
     -  Linear

Many of the comments point out how scary this game is. Personally, I agree it is scary but not like Amnesia scary (which on my scale is utterly terrifying). This game has a constant undertone of darkness and a nightmarish quality that bares its teeth all throughout the game, with moments of heightened terror which truly make the experience worthwhile while not being too terribly scary to be unable to play through it. 

The voiceover, trinkets, and pieces of correspondence that you discover throughout the game provide a very well-rounded way of understanding the madness that struck the artist and how his colleagues around him reacted. The soundtrack is superb, and at one point I had to stop momentarily to enjoy the piece that played over a particular part of the game. 

Overall, Layers of Fear overflows with beauty and tragedy, and I'm glad to have been able to experience this piece of art. To the developers: You're one of the good ones. Thank you for your ongoing contribution to indie games.

[i]Layers Of Fear[/i] is a game quite unlike any other. To add a bit of backstory, I purchased the game in Early Access back in October 2015 after being intrigued by the original idea and was instantly blown away by the amount of polish there was in an unreleased game. Even in its unfinished state, [i]Layers Of Fear[/i] had gorgeous graphics, a well-designed story and campaign, and even a fun event for Halloween (which i accidentally got stuck in.. but besides the point). As time went on, updates changed the game and added new rooms to gameplay, which made the game replayable with every update because there was always new stuff to find.

After being so thoroughly impressed with the Early Access version, I was ecstatic when the final product came out. I restarted the game from the beginning and found myself enjoying it just as much as I had the first time around. In [i]Layers Of Fear[/i], you play as a painter who buries himself away in his house, going mad as he desperately tries to finish his final masterpiece. Without spoiling too much, the game has extremely sad undertones and tells a very tragic story, should you choose to listen. However, many players won't have the gut to scavenge for story items due to how terrifying and fast paced the game is. Although [i]Layers Of Fear[/i] can be described as a "walking simulator," it's definitely anything but dull and boring. Most of the game revolves around the mechanic of things changing behind your back while you're not looking. The entire experience is played out without a single loading screen, and this entire idea is pulled off extremely well. That being said, if you find it difficult to maneuver the world and control the camera angles in 3D games, this one may simply not be for you. Many of the scares require you to look at a certain place at a certain time, which is quite easy to do if you're used to video games, but if you aren't so good with 3D, the full effect of the game may be lost on you.

Now let's talk about the scares themselves -  you can't have a good horror game without it being scary, right? Now let me say just one thing: this game is absolutely terrifying. If it isn't the scariest game I've ever played, then it's still in my top 3, no questions asked. The gorgeous graphics and flawless sound design create a gripping atmosphere at all times, and there was never a moment in the entire campaign where I wasn't on the edge of my seat, waiting to see what was going to happen next. The best thing this game has going for it is that it's original. While games like [i]Outlast[/i] (2013) had you running away from horrific beasts in gruesome locations, [i]Layers Of Fear[/i]'s horror is very different. Some may say that [i]Layers[/i] is filled with cheap jumpscares, but it really isn't. While the jumps are frequent, it's really the psychedelic aspect that brought out the fear in me. It's extremely difficult to explain how the scares work in this game, but even the trailers don't do it justice. This game will have you spinning in circles and watching the entire room change with every rotation. It's no joke. The jumpscares, along with the psychedelic elements and the changing rooms behind every door, will have you trembling each time you open a door at night for weeks. Not to mention that the game generally moves at a brisk pace, with a kind of BOOM scare, move to next room, BOOM another scare, etc etc, which makes it all the more terrifying each time you run away from something right into something else. I wouldn't watch too many videos on this game before playing it to get a feel for what I'm saying though, because when you see all the scares a room has to offer before you enter it, they can be a little less exciting.

Unfortunately, there were a few moments in the game where doing something can become ever so slightly tedious or repetitive ([spoiler]THE PART WITH THE CHECKERBOARD NEAR THE END OH MY GOD[/spoiler]), which pulls you out of the moment. In a game that's very atmosphere-centric, this can be a problem, if not only a minor one. It's also worth mentioning that the game features quite a few cleverly designed puzzles that feel challenging, but never unfair. One thing I didn't like about the update to the final game was that it added female narrative along with the player's own thoughts, which made it seem less introspective and personal. The fact that there was only one actual character with a voice actor in the game made it feel quite lonely and added to the experience. Although this is only an opinion, I feel it was important to add for the sake of being thorough.

[h1]TL;DR/OVERVIEW[/h1]
[b]Overal Score: 9/10[/b]
All in all, Layers Of Fear is a horror game I know I won't soon forget. With a completely original concept (something the horror genre overall has been lacking lately), unique scare tactics, clever puzzles and a fantastic atmosphere, Bloober Team has definitely hit the nail on the head with this one. The game is also highly replayable, as there are hundreds of cabinets to open and tons of things to find, as well as rooms that you can't visit by playing through the game only once.

I get that super immersive, very story heavy games like this aren't for everyone, and I can see how after a few chapters, it might start to feel a bit worn out.. but there's a lot to be said about experiencing the visual story telling of this game for the first time. LoF had left a profound impression on me five years ago, when I first played it. I was impressed with the mechanics of the game and it's non-euclidean setting, which at the time I personally hadn't really experienced a game that used them in a horror setting like this... there's a lot of really fun, unsettling visual story telling here. I found the story of the protagonist and his dissent into madness very compelling. The sound design, and particularly the score itself, are beautiful and chilling. I revisited this game for the first time since it's initial release (I had only played it once before, when it had first come out) and I found new secrets I hadn't found before...it had the same sort of effect as it did back in 2016: I turned off my computer, crawled into bed and ended up staring at my ceiling into the wee hours of the night, thinking about it for hours.

Horror games have been having a lot of trouble, as of late. They are usually very gimmicky and often times extremely predictable. Very little do we see actual psychological horror done correctly anymore. The last two horror games I have loved have been Outlast: Whistleblower and Amnesia: The Dark Descent. There's a bit of a time gap there. And before that, it was Silent Hill 2 so we've been lacking in good horror games. I miss the Oh, sh*t moments of games like Condemned: Criminal Origins when paths were being blocked behind you and mannequins had replaced that open space to loosen you up with unease before a hobo attacked you. Sound silly? Well, it is until you're playing it. But it hadn't much been tried before that and it was delivered well. The originality of it payed off. 

Now, where does Layers of Fear come in? Psychological Horror brought back to form. Think back to the Silent Hill series. Yes, many were terrible but I still remember the moment when I realized, "This f**king staircase is infinite..." and turned around. This game does it constantly; nearly to the point of being a gimmick. It's actually really quite unsettling. You start realizing that once that door closes behind you, you've nowhere to go but forward. The atmosphere is perfect and it's visually a treat to play. A few mechanical problems with the loading sometimes but nothing that takes away from the game. The way that the story is delivered is something of a treat as well. It hands you just enough in voice acting for you to get it but if you really want the dark story behind you game, you will read read read and it's very very good stuff. 

Now, there are some issues with this game. The main one that gets to me, even if I know that there's no real solution unless they wanted to lose some aspects of this work; the sense of danger. They bring it to you and hand it to you on a silver platter but even the most minute thought of what the games mechanics are shatters the emotion. I'm claustrophobic and this game really exploited that at one point. Shadows were closing in around me, forcing me to, if I wanted my sanity, go toward this still life painting of fruit which, for *ehem* reasons was actually very terrifying, but yet, the next set of rooms were supposed to make you look over your shoulder but yet, you knew that because of the nature of this game, there's no health bar or real sprint feature. It isn't going to Amnesia you and force you to hide in a closet. It plays with phobias, not fight or flight. Now, I said this is a bad thing but really only for people who aren't readily affected by that kind of scare. If you are totally immersed and you are okay with letting your imagination run wild with this game, you will be more than serviced by this game. You'll need to take breathers as I have had to. 

Second gripe, the voice acting is serviceable. It's pretty okay but one listen to the opening monologue will turn you off a little. It does get better but sometimes, you just have to really read the subtitles and think of the image instead of the delivery. Small gripe, though.

One last thing, when this game isn't messing with your inner fears, it's jump scaring you. I hate jump scares. I think they're cheap....but this game doesn't make me hate them. It builds tension and really forces you into the world, like it or not. I'll forgive it. 

Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. But only if you have an open mind to what Psychological horror is in gaming. Is it survival horror by any means? No, not really. Does it make you feel like running, yes, at times, but is there anything behind you? Odds are, no. But it'll still gnaw at you and make you hate that you want to look. 


Also, d*mn, the artist for this game was amazing.

"Hey, it's about painting! It must be classy and profound."

"No inventory or user interface?  That means a truly immersive experience, pared down to the essentials!"

"No combat or death?  Sounds like a psychological thriller, with lots of atmosphere and nuanced story."

Not so fast.

This game's pretty sneaky about tricking you into thinking that it's doing way more than it actually is. Hate to say it, but scrape away the superficial gloss of the artistic theme and visual flair and there's not much underneath.
  
I mean, what are you really doing here besides walking through a big house and waiting for the next loud noise to startle you?
   
There's no fighting and no danger.  You follow a more or less linear path, so there's no meaningful exploration, either.  You interact with items here and there but you don't solve real puzzles.  All of the key events happened in the past, and so a cryptic scrapbook of vague hints, allusions and recollections is all that connects you to the characters while you stumble around in confusion, never sure what's real and what's in your head.
  
As the player, you start to wonder why they need you here at all.
  
The main thing it has going for it is the visual presentation, which can be pretty creative.  They do this thing where they change the scene behind your back without warning you and then force you to turn around and notice that everything's different.  Objects appear and disappear; passages open up or close off; rooms turn from normal to scary looking, that sort of stuff.  It happens pretty often so you start to expect it; but while it could have become gimmicky it was handled well enough that I thought it was a nice touch.  It added to the feeling of disorientation and created a surreal atmosphere in a unique way. 
 
Besides that, there's the standard array of creepy imagery.  You've got your bloodstains and dolls and ominous writing on the walls; your melty faces and screaming spirits and dark holes that you don't want to jump down but you do it anyway.  It's not bad, but I think it suffers from the same problem as Concluse.  They overload you with so many horrors so fast, everybody's already so tortured and miserable that before long you're numb to the whole spectacle. 
 
It's really typical of these walking simulator horror games in general.  The less stuff there is for you to do, the less stake you have in anything that happens.  You need to feel like you have some skin in the game to create real tension.
  
Oh well.  They say art is never appreciated in its time so it might just take a few hundred years, or at least until it's on sale for under 5 bucks. Whichever comes first.

Take P.T., Eraserhead, Picture of Dorian Gray, Jan Svankmajer (google him), and an art history textbook. Put them in a blender with a heavy dose of optical illusions and shadows. Garnish with a paprika of some pretty good jump-scares. That's this game.  A 3 hour victorian themed take on 'what if P.T. were a full game.' I mean that in a good way because this is a very obviously lovingly crafted experience built around gameplay ideas in the infamous P.T./Silent Hills demo.

Pros:
-Amazing visuals, including some really cool optical illusion stuff.
-Gloriously dreadful atmosphere.
-Very nice sound design (play with surround sound headphones if you can - the bass is a big deal at some parts)
-Some genuine jump-scares that got my adrenaline pumping against my will.
-Amazing payoff at the ending with some really cool animation.
-Didn't experience any bugs except an extremely minor one after the ending just before the credit rolls. (A cabinet suddenly teleported closed while I had my head wedged looking in it.)
-The first time I've ever been unnerved by receiving an achievement.  (You will know which one I am talking about when you get it.)

Cons:
-Much of the writing in the backstory items and dialogue is unconvincing and doesn't sound authentically period at all. For a game with so much attention to detail, this stood out as disappointing for me.
-Some puzzles grind the game to a halt for a bit, leaving you doing some boring pixel-hunting for numbers you might have overlooked, and repeating a particular part as you do.
-Some cheap eye-rolling unscary scares.
-Lapses into cliche in its story quite a lot. I also feel like a much meatier story could have elevated this game more.
-Only 3 hours long. It's a good and memorable 3 hours, but for $20 some people may want to wait till a sale. I got it because it has subject matter up my alley (art history nerd) so you may want to get it for the same reasons I did tho.

Layers of Fear is an experience of the most terrifying kind - the spiraling descent into madness.  The Artist, who is determined to regain his lost artistic genius by completing his Magnum Opus, also struggles with the horrific truths surrounding himself and his family.  As he gets closer and closer to completing his masterpiece, layer by layer, you, the player, uncover his past sins and the repercussions thereof, again, layer by layer.  The culimnation of his terrifying journey is determined by your choices, as the game's multiple endings depend entirely on your interactions within his utterly broken mind.   

A true psychological horror, Layers of Fear isn't about combating evil or running from monsters.  It's about the Artist facing his own personal demons head on; you can hear them crying, scratching at the walls, lumbering down the hallways, pounding on the door. It also doesn't rely on cheap jump scares, although there are scares in abundance, they are authentic and relevant to the story.  The atmosphere, while always unsettling, can quickly alternate between dark and oppressive to bright and almost cheerful, but don't allow such changes to lull you into a false sense of security; the Artist's mind is a twisting labrynth of terror, prone to metamorphosis at a moment's notice. 

Multiple endings, collectibles and secrets that will only unlock after a complete playthrough, or if a specific ending has been achieved, add to the replay value.  I plan to revist the Artist and his nightmarish world often.

TL;DR: Hauntingly beautiful atmosphere, an intriguing storyline, spine tingling SFX and horrifying hallucinations coalesce into a masterpiece (no pun intended) of the horror genre. If you're a horror fan, you need this game in your life.

To start off, I haven't played the DLC. This is a review of the base game. I bought this game way back when it first came out as early-release, and recently played it again as a full game. Figured I would review it now that it's been released for over a year. Kudos to the developers for working on the game consistently, and actually following through to final release. That doesn't happen often with early release titles. 

I really wanted to love this game. And I think that for what this game is, it's okay. But it falls short on a lot of promises and certainly doesn't live up to what the developers claim it is. Like many others in the comments section, I was craving the experience that the PT demo promised. This game tried to be a "spiritual successor" to PT, and in that regard fell oh so very short. I can enjoy games without comparing them to others or expecting them to live up to unrealistic standards, but this game doesn't have a leg to stand on; all expectations aside.

Here's what's wrong with the game:

- Very short story. This was the case with the early-release version, and is still the case with the full release.

- Overpriced. When I bought this game originally, I think it was in the realm of $10? Now as a final release, it's $21. The price increase would make sense, had the developers meaningfully increased the content. But they didn't.

- Which brings me to my next point, not a whole lot has changed between early release and the final product. Sure, the game is more polished now, and there are a few more hallways and rooms to walk through, but that's it. 95% of the game stayed exactly the same. So much so, that I was able to predict every "scare" along the way from when I first played this game (which was a long time ago). 

- Very linear story. This one actually bugs me a lot, because at the beginning of the game it tells you that "this is your journey" and "every decision you make changes the outcome". That's bologna. There is simply zero actual choice in this game. Of all the rooms and hallways with multiple doors, only one opens. Sometimes a second door opens, but only to reveal a piece of paper or a 2spooky4me chair facing a wall. It's a dead end and you still have to go down the same path either way. The story and order of everything was THE SAME as when I first played this game in early release. Anyone with two brain cells can play 30 minutes into this game and realise that the story is 100% linear and pre-determined. Shame on the devs for claiming otherwise.

- Spo0o0o0ky jump scares. That's really all this game is. Jump scares and stuff warping, which most of the time has nothing to do with the story or game. The scares take different forms, but it's all the same. It gets really predictable and repetitive after the first hour of gameplay. The atmosphere does a poor job of immersing you, and the story is boring and convoluted. At no point is this game legitimately scary.

- Last but not least, zero replay value. As I mentioned already, this game was damn near identical to what I played in early release. The "scary" moments were all the same, the rooms were the same, the progression was the same. There was the odd extra room or hallway, but that's it. And despite having played this game such a long time ago, I knew everything that was going to happen. Nothing surprised me, nothing stood out. So this game really is only playable one time for the very short (maybe 4 hour) campaign. After that, you may as well uninstall it. 

So if you're looking for a one and done, short, overpriced, predictable walking simulator with 0 replay value, and predicatable and cliche jump scares, then this is the game for you. But if you're looking for a good horror game and want to actually be scared and immersed in a good story, and not just startled repeatedly, then look elsewhere.

I think I spent almost an hour in the first few rooms just wandering about, marvelling at pictures, opening and closing the tap in the bathroom, appreciating the ineffable beauty of such simple things as fruits and vegetables lying in complete disorder on the countertop in the kitchen – I knew that at some point I would need to make progress, but rushing it felt like sacrilege. I wanted to savour the incredible atmosphere, relish the wonderful soundtrack and immerse myself as much as possible in the life of a distraught painter. On a side note, I think I achieved my goal, having finished the entire game in one sitting, absolutely riveted to the screen. But...  

The developers set the bar a bit too high, and that standard was impossible to maintain throughout the game. It soon became lacklustre, as I realised that the gameplay primarily consists of facing a locked door, turning around, getting scared by a painting or a bunch of books flying in your face, turning around yet again to see that the door can now be opened, going through it and repeating the same thing every five minutes, occassionally solving a simple puzzle and sitting through a nightmarish sequence of grotesque visuals (to be fair, I don't have anything to say against the latter – most scenes were very creative.) However, the jumpscares soon become predictable and annoying: there are way too many of them and they serve no purpose whatsoever. The story is sickening enough on its own, some pictures are genuinely unnerving, and the music ties it all together in a morbid blend of madness and self-destruction – this would already be a horror game without any jarring sounds and "creepy" dolls suddenly tumbling from the cupboard.

Still, there were [b]many[/b] things I absolutely admired, like the rat sketches – they did a sterling job at conveying how mentally unstable our protagonist is, the notes that I read and re-read over and over again because of how well-written they are, the sinister yet doleful music and the stellar voice acting, among other features – all these are the reasons why I recommend this game to anyone despite its shortcomings. I won't forget that first enchanting impression and the feeling of being swept away by something so new and unique.

Layers of fear is a First Person Walking Simulator, where you are an artist inside your manor. The purpose is to end your Ultimate Portrait, and for this you will wander around your mansion. The problem is that strange events and hallucinations will happen while you will go around looking for the elements necessary for your Final Opera.

Most of the game structure is not logical, you don't know what to expect, you don't know how to react, you don't know if you should turn around or not and personally this is mostly the reason this game inspired me such fear and anguish for it.

The game has been developed in Unity and I have to say the quality of the design, ambience and effects is really impressive, considering the indie development team. Unfortunately there's always a splash launch screen before the game itself, probably used to launch the DLC (which I won't play, as the game itself was definitely enough for me XD). Too bad it seems a little buggy as it takes a lot for it to load pictures and text in it (fortunately the launch button is loaded immediately).

[h1][u]Paint by Nightmares[/u][/h1]

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[b]This is a mixed review that doesn’t have entirely nicey-nice things to say, and if I could give the game a star rating, it’d be 3.5 out of 5.[/b]
I bought this game during Early Acess and reviewed it then. I wasn't as detailed as I would have liked. Now that the game is fully released, I'd like to reassess my opinion of it... because while the game is amazing in a lot of ways, it also disappointed me in other areas. Layers of Fear really shines in the horror genre for stepping away from the survival action aspect and comes forward to being completely story-driven, but what it gains in storytelling, it lacks in horrifying me in the way I hoped.
I have played the game multiple times during Early Access, and completed the fully-released game once.

[h1]The Positives[/h1]
1) The story itself. It’s deliciously dark. I might be a little biased when it comes to enjoying the story, because like the protagonist, I'm also an artist, so it spoke to me in ways other horror games don't. The main story has a very cryptic nature to it, and it doesn't come right out and tell you what's going on-- you figure it out on your own by inspecting letters and items. I enjoy that kind of writing.

2) The "insane" feeling you get when wandering the house. My favorite kind of horror is psychological, as I don't believe in ghosts or demons, and therefore don't find them scary. So, as you might imagine, I'm very tired of games or movies involving demons or possessions or haunted houses. This game seems to be almost entirely a mind-trip, as it plays off of what you might consider common for a game to have or include, then changes it. It surprises you by throwing twists and angles you didn't expect, thus giving you the feeling you are "going insane". I loved that feeling, and it made me love the game.

3) The visuals and sound were done very well. That goes without saying when complimenting its nuanced style of psychologically-influenced gameplay, but they also look amazing in other areas. The lighting is perfect at times, as are the many paintings on the walls. The sound is haunting and creeps its way into your brain with eerie, low piano music, hums and static fizzles. Playing this game with headphones on seems almost necessary. That voice acting, though… it’s all right, but not the best.

[h1]The Negatives[/h1]
1) I hate saying "such and such part of the game was easy!" because it insults anyone who got stuck on a particular part of the game, which I find to be tasteless. Some things are obvious to people in games, and for others, we overthink it, because we assume to be in a game that's more complicated than it is. I have fallen victim to this trap many times.

In my personal opinion, the “puzzles” weren’t challenging enough. I don't even think they should be considered "puzzles," because they required almost no solving. Usually the solution was something like "turn on light switch" or "light the candle" in order to see a certain number or letter on the wall. Maybe the game didn't intend to be heavy on the puzzles, so I can't blame it [i]too[/i] much for this. It’s likely they didn’t want the game’s precious, though minimal three hours of time to be bogged down by “solving” things. I’ll give it a slight pass on this one, since the quick, simple feeling of the game might be my personal preference to be challenged by something.

2) The Silent Hills P.T. has influenced this game a [i]lot[/i], and while that isn't really a negative... there were some things that felt directly ripped off of it. [spoiler]Like Ghost Wife leaping at you and grabbing your face and shaking her head around like she's on twenty ounces of speed.[/spoiler]. While I never played the P.T., I did watch playthroughs of it, and honestly, it was in a class all its own. Others can mimic it, but it felt like it did something right. And even just watching those playthroughs terrified me more than playing this game did.

3) Jump scares aren't scary. Maybe other people disagree with me on that, but I've never been afraid of them. Yeah, I jump when something goes "BWWWAAAH!" because that's an organic response. I don't feel "scared" afterward. I just feel annoyed. Layers of Fear uses [i]mostly[/i] jump scares to deliver its horror to you. While I loved the "insanity" feeling mentioned above, I hate that it just used generic methods of scaring you rather than make something look and feel horrifying just by looking at it and feeling horrified. There are the occasional "Whoa, that's effed up" paintings that have creepy, grimacing faces that send chills down my spine, but those moments are rare, and honestly, there wasn’t nearly enough of that. I wanted more of the “good god, that painting is watching me” rather than the “BOO! GOTCHA!”

4) I've beaten the game and I still don't know any of the characters' names. Would be nice to feel as though I was part of an identity so that I could relate to them. If you [i]can[/i] learn their names, and I just didn't manage do, forgive this note. However, I don't think finding out the name of the [i][b]character you play[/b][/i] should be a mystery.

5) There are multiple endings to the game (3 to be exact), but there's no way to know how to get them unless you look it up online and possibly spoil it for yourself. I hate games that do this. I already know the other endings, and I know how to get them-- but I had to look up what I was supposed to do (and thus spoiled them for myself, so I have no reason to replay the game). This is also an indication that to get the more "complete" of endings, you need walkthroughs to know where to pick up the items (because it isn't always very clear). I was as thorough as I could possibly be in my previous playthrough and I still somehow missed a lot of items.

6) Game length is shorter than what I'm used to. The fully-completed game took me about three hours. Twenty bucks… for three hours. Just no. Get it on sale.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
While I do have a lot of nitpicks, I still recommend Layers of Fear to all horror fans. Why? Well, mostly because it's unique, and tries to do something new (well, new-ish). It's not an FPS, it's not an action game, it's not even a survival game (which seem to plague the market these days). It's a story-based game, and when all said and done, it is [i]good[/i] at telling the story. I do wish, however, that the game had been more atmospheric, and less predictable in its execution. And I know this might sound stupid to some people… but I wish it was scarier.

This game really freaks me out, in a good way. It gets progressively more disturbing after each door you open, so it has the perfect build up. Also, when you die, you get thrown into the next area rather than having to restart and do the same thing over again, which I found extremely refreshing. It keeps you immersed rather than frustrated.

This game is an artful demonstration of how some stories can only be told in specific media. Layers of Fear tells the story of tragedy, addiction and mental illness and spins them into a tale of true horror. If you like suspense, beautiful animation, creepy claustrophobic environments and the sensation that you're slowly slipping into madness, this game is for you.
This game is about obsession, and how truly dark, disgusting, and depressing it can be when you lose yourself in your own creation.

While Layers of Fearhas wonderful visuals and the sound design can be quite good at times, the rest of the game falls short. The story is fairly banal and for something labeled as psychological horror you'd expect more from its narrative. Its easy to discern the direction the story is going from the first 15 minutes. It's also hard to take the game seriously when the narrator's lines and delivery are so painfully bad. There are also multiple endings, but all save for one will almost certainly require a walkthrough (which is what everyone wants to do when they're playing a horror game, right?) and none of them are even remotely satisfying. 

Lastly we have the gameplay which is virtually non-existant, walk around the house occasionally interact with things or find some letter's from the protagonist's past, it's stuff you see in every game of this ilk and it does nothing to evolve this stagnant formula. There's a small handful of "puzzles" but they ask very little of the player. Layer of Fear does have some neat psychological horror tricks up its sleeve, but they get reused ad nauseum (things like when you turn around you find the scenery behind you has changed) and I've seen them so many times before this that even the initial novelty is meager to say the least. The game is also incredibly short, a little over two hours for me, which would be fine if either the price was lower or the game was significantly better; see What Remains of Edith Finch for a perfect example of a two hour game that justifies its pricetag.

I don't like that I don't like this game, it does have some neat ideas, but it's a bit messy and too predictable in its execution. The dev team is releasing a sequel soon which can hopefully improve upon this game's foundation but the fact that game is going to be $30 at launch is already cause for concern in my eyes.

Layers of fear are well explained. The game is the ninth art. The classical soundtrack and delicate pictures take you to the game world very well. The painter is crazy, but his world is more colorful.  The lines that outline are not paintings, but a lonely and greedy heart in a crazy state.

I really wanted to enjoy Layers of Fear; however, it unfortunately failed to capture my interest or scare me for that matter.

Some positives to mention about the game:
- Technically it's good. The graphics are pleasing to look at, and the soundscape is acceptable.
- The voice acting is very good.
- The game makes use of a lot of good literary symbolism that I found interesting.

Some negatives:
- Some of the contrast between light and dark effects is disorienting.
- A lot of the jump scares are choreographed well in advance leaving little to the imagination.
- There's an over-reliance on stock sound effects during scenes or sections that are presumably intended to be scary.
- The overall plot of uncovering fragments of a shattered psyche is "cliche" and overdone.
- One technical problem is that the UI of the menu and settings for the game is stiff.
- Mechanically, the gameplay is very stiff. I got the feeling that I was watching from the perspective of a camera attached to a broomstick rather than an actual person.

I don't think that the game is horrible - it's just very cliche and mechanically weak. I think that some people might like it, but I don't recommend it.

I’ve never written a review before, but this game feels like it deserves a few words.

In Layers of Fear, you step into the shoes of a painter trying to complete his magnum opus or his “great work.”

As you move through the game, you slowly begin to understand his descent into madness. I won’t say more about the story. It’s something you should experience for yourself.

What I will share is a personal realization this game left me with.

As an aspiring artist, a writer and a painter, I found something unsettlingly familiar in it. We often talk about the sacrifices required to create something meaningful, but we rarely stop to consider what that truly means.

In trying to create something "perfect", we find ourselves pushing our own sanity in isolation. We sacrifice time with the people we love, only to sit and stare at that same creator’s block we’ve faced so many times before.

To me, the game doesn’t just portray madness. It reflects something far more personal: the obsession with perfection and the inability to achieve it. The feeling that what you’re making will never be enough, no matter how much of yourself you pour into it.

At some point, it felt too familiar. And it stopped feeling like horror.

Layers of Fear is essentially a walking simulator, albeit a very good one. The horror aspects are modeled very closely to the playable teaser from Hideo Kojima and Guillermo del Toro, otherwise known a PT, wherein your character is trapped in a house with a vengeful ghost, and your goal is make it through.

Graphically the game is beautiful, as long as your PC is up to snuff, everything is well detailed and pops with vibrance; from the general house itself, to the black, inky corruption that slowly engulfs the husband's sanity.

Jump-scares are the primary go-to for the game's horror element, and although they're often predictable, there were several times when things got quiet, and I honestly felt unnerved and tense.

The faults I find come from the controls, and the game's length. Similar to another series by Frictional Games, Layers of Fear attempts to use a grab and pull mechanic, where you click an object, and then move your mouse in order to open doors, cabinets, and solve puzzles. Although I enjoy the control in general, It isn't as polished as Soma or Amnesia.

The other problem, and it's only a minor one, is the game's length. Even taking your time, you can finish it in a few hours. Depending on your preference, this may not be an issue, but personally, I like my games to be a little longer. 

Those issues aside, I really enjoyed the game! It might be a walking simulator with a few puzzles, but Layers of fear is still worth your time.

I never had such mixed feelings for a game before I played Layers of Fear. The first hour of it was absolutely exhilarating, props to the devs for absolutely nailing the bone-chilling atmosphere. Jump scares were minimal and the ever-changing layout of the protagonist's mansion helped alleviate the theme of insanity. I honestly regarded the game as one of the best horror games ever made, making even the likes of Amnesia pale in comparison. 

Then, I got bored. The repetitiveness of the game did not bring out a sense of fear as it initially did, but instead brought out one of boredom. 2 hours in, and I didn't give a crap about the obviously painstakingly crafted environment, the changing layouts of the house and even the jump scares, and that wasn't all because of the repetitive nature of the game, about halfway through the game, there was a scene involving a ghost baby running into a drawer, how anyone found that to be even the least bit scary is beyond me. From then on, I failed to take the game seriously, the "babyface" artwork that intentionally sent shivers down my spine for being disturbing soon descended to be nothing more than a funny face. 

The thing which Outlast and Amnesia got right is that they never showed their hand too early on, they always had something new to offer. Granted, Layers of Fear had me more terrified than either game, but as I mentioned earlier, this fear faded away to boredom, whereas Outlast and Amnesia had in me a sense of dread, a sense of actual fear, from the beginning, all the way to the end, and that was probably due to the actual threat the enemies faced in both games. The antagonist in Layers of Fear was nothing more than a jump scare machine. With the realization that there is no actual threat to the player, Layers of Fear soon became nothing more than a walking simulator with jumpscares added for good measure.

All in all, I really wanted to like this game, and I did, at first. Unfortunately, Layers of Fear is nothing more than a sad case of wasted potential. The story is pretty decent but the gameplay really really gets boring after a while, and the "sanity"-like aspect of the game becomes a dumb gimmick at a certain point in the game. Also, I want to point out that this game has 3 endings. Sorry devs, but I think a single playthrough is enough for me.
